title: TB4-08995
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the principal Appellant), his children XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, his sister XXXX XXXX (the associated Appellant), and her daughter XXXX XXXX XXXX, all citizens of Uganda, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the principal Appellant), his children XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, his sister XXXX XXXX (the associated Appellant), and her daughter XXXX XXXX XXXX, all citizens of Uganda, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection. They have submitted new evidence in support of their appeals. The Appellants ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the determination of the RPD and either accept their refugee claims or refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel. These appeals are allowed. Background

The principal Appellant alleged before the RPD that he was an activist for the rights of sexual minorities in Uganda, and also that he is bisexual, and that he and his children are at risk of persecution because of his human rights activities and his sexual orientation. The associated Appellant claimed that she was involved in the opposition Forum for Democratic Change in Uganda, and that she and her daughter face persecution as a result.

The principal Appellant came to Canada with the associated Appellant's daughter, who is allegedly his niece, in XXXX of 2013; the associated Appellant came to Canada with the principal Appellant's two children in XXXX of 2014. Although the adult Appellants came to Canada separately and made separate refugee claims, those claims were joined by the RPD and heard together.

The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration Canada (the Minister) intervened by documents in the associated Appellant's claim before the RPD. The Minister disclosed fingerprint and photographic evidence which suggests that the associated Appellant, who claims to be XXXX XXXX, born XXXX XXXX, 1977, is really XXXX XXXX, born XXXX XXXX XXXX 1980. That evidence also indicates that the associated Appellant has two children, neither named XXXX XXXX XXXX.1 The Minister asked the RPD to find that the associated Appellant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.

The Appellants' joined refugee claims were heard on July 3, 2014 and August 1, 2014. By a decision of September 2, 2014, the RPD rejected the claims. It found that the principal Appellant had not established with credible evidence that he is bisexual or that he was a human rights activist; it found that the other Appellants did not have the "personal identity and refugee experience alleged."2

The Appellants appealed to the RAD. They asked the RAD to disjoin the appeals of XXXX XXXX and her daughter from the others. A differently-constituted panel of the RAD denied this request, noting that RAD Rule 41 requires the joining of appeals where the corresponding refugee claims were joined before the RPD. That panel considered the factors set out in Rule 41(5) and dismissed the application to separate.
The Appellants also made a separate application to correct typographical errors in the appeal record;3 the RAD accepts these corrections.

The Appellants argue on appeal that the RPD made incorrect findings with respect to their evidence, erred in respect to their identity, and also made errors in considering their credibility. ANALYSIS Role of the RAD
What is the role of the RAD in considering an appeal against a decision of the RPD?
While the IRPA sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the lower tribunal.

The Federal Court, in Huruglica, considered the appropriate relationship between the RAD and the RPD.4 It found that the RAD erred in simply reviewing the RPD's decision on a standard of reasonableness, rather than conducting its own independent assessment of the Appellants' refugee claims. The Court held that the RAD's application of a reasonableness standard curtailed the tribunal's appellate role, contrary to the purpose of the RAD and the provisions of IRPA. In the Court's view, the RAD should not even engage in a standard of review analysis; rather, it should consider the purpose of the appellate tribunal, the statutory provisions, comparable expertise, and comparative appellate regimes. The Court held that the RAD is not restricted to intervening only in the event of a palpable and overriding error.5

The Appellants submit that the RAD must follow Huruglica, and engage in its own assessment of the evidence in order to determine whether the Appellants are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. They also argue that their new evidence suggests a full appeal based on that evidence, where no standard of review applies.

In Huruglica, the Court determined that the RAD is to conduct a "hybrid appeal". The RAD will therefore review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of the Appellant's refugee claim, deferring to the RPD only where the lower tribunal enjoys a particular advantage in reaching a conclusion. Where the RAD's assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own determination. The RPD's Findings The Principal Appellant's Children

The RPD wrote, "It is my view that the personal identity of the minor claimants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXXl has also not been established on the balance of probabilities. This finding is based on the documentary evidence and submissions filed by the Minister's counsel."6

This finding is difficult to understand. The RAD has carefully reviewed the documents filed and submissions made by the Minister to the RPD.7 The Minister did not raise concerns with the identities of the principal Appellant's children. The Appellants presented the RAD with passports in the names of these two children.8 If the RPD had reason to doubt the veracity of these documents, it was obligated to say so. Instead, the RPD simply found that the identity of these two children had not been established, based on documents and submissions that are not relevant to the children. This was an error.

There may indeed be issues regarding the identity of these particular Appellants. They arrived in Canada with the associated Appellant, who is not their parent, and whose own identity may be in question. Someone who is linked by fingerprints and a photograph to the associated Appellant made an application for a Canadian visa and listed two children-with the same birthdates and similar names as these minor Appellants-as her own son and daughter. The RAD, not having seen the children, is in no position to make a finding in respect of their identity. Therefore, the issue of identity will need to be considered by another panel of the RPD; if that panel finds that identity has been established, it must also consider whether these minor Appellants are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. The Associated Appellant and Her Daughter

The associated Appellant arrived in Canada with the principal Appellant's children. She claimed to be XXXX XXXX, born XXXX XXXX, 1977, and confirmed that she has never used any other name. She also claimed that she is married to XXXX XXXX, born XXXX XXXX, 1979, and that XXXX XXXX XXXX, born XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, is her daughter.9 She was assisted by counsel in preparing the Basis of Claim (BoC) form and confirmed that the information therein was complete, true, and correct.

The Minister obtained biometric information for XXXX XXXX, showing a birthdate of XXXX XXXX, 1979. This information, when shared with U.S. authorities, revealed that the fingerprints belonged to an individual named XXXX XXXX, born XXXX XXXX, 1978, who had applied for a U.S. visa. Immigration records show that Mr. XXXX married XXXX XXXX in January of 2014.

Immigration records for XXXX XXXX show that she applied for a Canadian visa in XXXX of 2014, but was refused. This application included a photograph which, in the Minister's submission, looks very similar to the associated Appellant. The visa application listed two children: a daughter, XXXX XXXX, born XXXX XXXX, 2007, and a son, XXXX XXXX, born XXXX XXXX, 2009.10

Here the RAD must note that the principal Appellant came to Canada in XXXX of 2013 with the associated Appellant's alleged daughter, XXXX XXXX XXXX. The associated Appellant remained in Uganda, and later came to Canada XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX -born XXXX XXXX XXXX 2007-and XXXX XXXX XXXX, born XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009. To summarize: before the associated Appellant came to Canada, and at the time the principal Appellant was already in Canada, someone with a very similar picture, and linked to her by her alleged husband's fingerprints, made an application in Uganda for a Canadian visa, listing two children as her own, though they have the same birthdates and first names as the children of the principal Appellant. When the principal appellant's children later were successful in obtaining visas, they applied with another woman, not related to them.11

It was quite appropriate for the RPD to consider such factors, but the panel was required to go farther. The RPD is presumed to have considered all of the evidence before it, and there is no requirement for the panel to refer to each document in the record.12 However, where there is evidence which is contrary to its decision, the RPD must analyze that evidence and provide reasons why it does not consider it relevant or trustworthy, or why it chose to disregard it.13 Here, as the Appellants point out, the associated Appellant presented a passport to the RPD, and she claims this was genuine.14 The RPD was required to consider this document in determining the associated Appellant's identity. Instead, it made no reference to the passport, and this was an error.

The RPD also found that the identity of XXXX XXXX XXXX, the associated Appellant's alleged daughter, had not been established. The RAD does have concerns about the identity of this child: she did not come to Canada with her own parent, and the individual who claims to be her mother has some unresolved issues in respect to her own identity. However, in considering this minor Appellant's identity, the RPD was required to take her passport into consideration. Its failure to do so was an error.

The RPD was wrong to ignore the passports of the associated Appellant and her daughter in making its finding on identity. The RAD, however, is not in a good position to make its own findings of identity here, not having seen or questioned any of the Appellants. This matter must therefore be remitted to the RPD for reconsideration.

The associated Appellant raises other challenges to the RPD's findings. As this matter is to be remitted back to the RPD for redetermination, it is not necessary for the RAD to consider each such issue. However, there is one issue which the RAD will address. The associated Appellant contends that she had difficulty understanding the Swahili-English interpreter in the RPD hearing, and claims that the interpreter mixed up dates and words. The RAD has some difficulty with this argument. The associated Appellant, when interviewed by immigration officials, stated that she was fluent in English and did not require an interpreter.15 She also indicated in her BoC that she speaks English.16 Although she alleges on appeal that the interpretation in the RPD hearing was inadequate, she has presented no evidence, such as an interpretation audit, to corroborate this allegation. The RAD does not accept that the Appellant's testimony before the RPD was in any way compromised by the interpretation. The Principal Appellant

The RPD accepted the principal Appellant's personal and national identity, but concluded that he had not established his sexual orientation or his profile as a human rights activist. There are a number of serious problems with the RPD's credibility findings here.

The RPD noted evidence that "LGBTI activists and vocal opponents of the state are subject to serious harm in Uganda." It went on to find that the principal Appellant had not established that he had ever been subject to such mistreatment.17 The panel subsequently wrote that "If XXXX XXXX had the degree and length of activism alleged, then more likely than not, he would have sustained serious harm, something not reliably shown to have occurred in his case."18 The RPD's reasoning here seems to be: activists in Uganda are seriously harmed, but this Appellant has not been seriously harmed, and therefore he was not an activist. With respect, this type of reasoning is neither logical nor based in the evidence. There is no evidence of which the RAD is aware, which establishes that each and every activist in Uganda has been subject to harm. The fact that the Appellant has, to date, escaped serious harm does not logically lead to the conclusion that he was not an activist. Further, the Convention refugee definition is forward-looking-there is simply no requirement that a claimant prove past persecution in order to establish a refugee claim.

The principal Appellant provided the RPD with an article from what the panel described as "a prominent regional newspaper, The Daily Monitor."19 The article was written by a former friend of the principal Appellant; the author wrote that word is starting to spread that XXXX XXXX is gay. The RPD acknowledged that "Uganda is highly homophobic and the new law compounds the danger to the LGBTI community and those seen to be closely associated with it." The panel also accepted that the article appeared in the newspaper as alleged. Despite this, the RPD found that "it has not been established on balance that it would expose XXXX XXXX to a serious possibility of sustaining the serious harm of persecution were he to return to Uganda. It has not been established on sufficient reliable evidence that XXXX XXXX is a LGBTI activist."20

It is difficult to follow the RPD's reasoning here. The RPD found that Ugandan society is highly homophobic, that sexual minorities are endangered, and accepted that an article was published suggesting that the principal Appellant is gay. What is then the relevance of his identity as an LGBTI activist? The RPD seemed to entirely miss the significance of the article-that the Appellant might face persecution as a perceived homosexual. This too was an error.

When the principal Appellant arrived in Canada, he did not immediately make a refugee claim on the basis of his sexual orientation. In fact, when he did claim, he did not include his bisexuality in his BoC form, nor did he tell immigration officials when interviewed. He revealed this aspect of his claim mid-hearing, after asking that his sister be excused from the hearing room. He told the RPD that he did not have the courage to come out as a bisexual earlier, and that at the time of the hearing he had not revealed his orientation to anyone else. The RPD concluded that the mid-hearing disclosure of the Appellant's bisexuality was not trustworthy, as he could have been expected to reveal this important information earlier.21

The RPD's finding here is defective because it simply does not engage the Appellant's explanation: that he comes from a society very hostile to sexual minorities, that he did not want his sister, also claiming refugee status in Canada, to know of his bisexuality, and that he continues to struggle with his bisexuality. The RPD's treatment of this matter is puzzling: "While I note that the general cultural complexities and considerations could be such as to explain XXXX XXXX conduct in not disclosing his alleged bisexuality before the hearing, it has not been established on sufficient reliable evidence and on the balance of probabilities that the very late and new mid-hearing disclosure of the allegations of XXXX XXXX bisexuality is trustworthy."22 As far as the RAD can understand this statement, it seems to say that the Appellant's cultural background could indeed explain his reluctance to reveal his sexual orientation-but the RPD would not accept such an explanation. It appears that the RPD, in one sentence, both accepted and rejected the Appellant's explanation for his late disclosure. No reason is given for the rejection of the explanation. This too was an error.

While the Appellants make further challenges to the credibility findings of the RPD, the errors discussed above are sufficient basis for the RAD to set aside the RPD's determination in respect to the principal Appellant.

The principal Appellant asks the RAD to find that he is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. The RAD is unable to do so. Despite the errors in the RPD's credibility findings, some credibility concerns remain. The Appellant completed immigration forms in which he declared that he has never been arrested or detained, though he alleges that in fact he was arrested on more than one occasion.23 Although he came to Canada in XXXX of 2013, allegedly already fearing persecution as LGBTI activist, he did not make a refugee claim until about five months later. And, in the RAD's view, the principal Appellant's credibility is also tied to the identity of the other Appellants. He claims that the associated Appellant is his sister and corroborates her identity; he claims that two of the minor Appellants are his children, and the other his niece. As set out above, the RAD has concerns about the identity of those Appellants, and the principal Appellant's own credibility is intertwined with those identity issues.
For these reasons, the principal Appellant's refugee claim must be referred back to the RPD for redetermination. Admissibility of Evidence Submitted on Appeal

Section 110(4) of IRPA provides that the Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claims or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected24 in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

It is for the Appellants to make full and detailed submissions in their Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of Section 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellants.25

While Section 110(4) provides the RAD with factors to consider in assessing a document's "newness," these factors alone cannot determine the admissibility of new evidence in an appeal. To put it simply, if a document is lacking in credibility, or is irrelevant, or is immaterial to the issues to be considered by the RAD, it would make little sense to admit such document, even if it meets the test in Section 110(4).

The RAD has, in many appeals to date, applied the factors set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in Raza.26 While Raza predates the introduction of IRPA Section 110(4), it is based on the nearly-identical wording of Section 113(a). The Court of Appeal held that new evidence should be considered for its credibility, relevance, newness, and materiality, in addition to any express statutory provisions.27

In Iyamuremye,28 the Federal Court accepted the RAD's application of the factors in Raza to new evidence submitted on an appeal under IRPA. Subsequently, in Ghannadi,29 the Court held that the RAD should consider the factors in Raza, but noted that these are merely considerations to be taken into account and not necessarily determinative of admissibility. Most recently the Court, in Singh,30 found that the factors in Raza are based specifically in the language of Section 113(a) and are not transferable in the context of an appeal before the RAD. The Court found that it was unreasonable for the RAD to strictly apply the Raza factors without distinguishing its own role from that of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) Officer who is bound by Section 113(a).

In Singh, the Court wrote that ...in order for there to be a "full fact-based appeal" before the RAD, the criteria for the admissibility of evidence must be sufficiently flexible to ensure it can occur. Often, the evidence at stake will be essential for proving the factual basis of the errors the claimant alleges were made by the RPD. This consideration becomes all the more pertinent in light of the strict timelines a claimant now faces for initially submitting evidence before the RPD. A claimant now has 50 days to present all documents from the date he or she made the claim; the previous legislative scheme required the documents 20 days prior to a hearing, which, on average, took much longer to take place. When the RPD confronts a claimant on the weakness of his evidentiary record, the RAD should, in subsequent review of the decision, have some leeway in order to allow the claimant to respond to the deficiencies raised.31

The Court also held that the "main issue is whether the evidence 'was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably (or normally according to the French version) have been expected in the circumstances to have presented.'"32

The Court did not discuss Iyamuremye or Ghannadi in its analysis of Sections 110(4) and 113(a). It did, however, certify the following question: "In considering the role of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment officer and that of the Refugee Appeal Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board, sitting in appeal of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division, does the test set out in Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 for the interpretation of paragraph 113(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 apply to its subsection 110(4)?"

While the certified question has not yet been answered, the RAD must nevertheless continue to consider new evidence, such as that which has been submitted in support of this appeal. While it may be inappropriate to strictly apply the factors in Raza, given that they are not specific to Section 110(4) and were not crafted for use in an appellate process, the RAD's consideration of new evidence cannot end with the application of the test in Section 110(4). To limit its analysis to that provision would be to ignore other provisions of IRPA-such as Sections 162(2) and 171(a.3)--as well as established jurisprudence based on statutory provisions almost identical to Section 110(4). Such a restricted analysis would also require the RAD to accept "new" evidence even if it is irrelevant, immaterial, or lacking in credibility.

The RAD presumes that Parliament, in creating Section 110(4), was well aware that this provision is almost identical in wording to Section 113(a)-which provides a strong indication that Parliament intended the test from Raza to be used by the RAD.33

The RAD will therefore undertake an analysis of any proposed new evidence, not only for its timeliness, which is largely the focus of Section 110(4), but also for its evidentiary value. In doing so, the RAD will look to the factors in Raza but will not be strictly bound by them, and in applying any Raza factors must distinguish its own role from that of a PRRA officer.

Section 171(a.3) of IRPA allows the RAD to receive and base a decision on evidence that is adduced in the proceedings and considered "credible or trustworthy in the circumstances." This provision makes it clear that, in addition to the factors in Section 110(4), the RAD must consider the credibility and trustworthiness of proposed new evidence.

While IRPA makes specific reference to the credibility of evidence received by the RAD, there is no corresponding provision which addresses relevance. However, in the RAD's view, it is obvious that evidence must be assessed for its relevance.34 Apart from the support from the case law, it would be highly inefficient for the RAD to admit irrelevant evidence, and contrary to Section 162(2) of IRPA, which requires all divisions of the IRB to "deal with all proceedings before it as informally and quickly as the circumstances and the considerations of fairness and natural justice permit."
It is therefore appropriate for the RAD to consider whether new evidence is relevant, even if it meets the test in Section 110(4).

The RAD will also consider whether the proposed new evidence is material. In Raza, the Federal Court of Appeal described this factor: "Is the evidence material, in the sense that the refugee claim probably would have succeeded if the evidence had been made available to the RPD? If not, the evidence need not be considered." This factor may, in the RAD's view, set an inappropriately high standard in the context of a RAD appeal.

An officer determining a PRRA application must not engage in a review of the applicant's negative RPD decision. The PRRA process exists to determine whether a risk to the applicant has arisen between the date of issue of the RPD's decision and the date of the applicant's pending removal from Canada,35 and the officer has no power to reconsider or set aside the RPD's decision. A PRRA will in most cases take place a year or more after the RPD's decision.36 In this context, the definition of materiality set out in Raza makes good sense: the new evidence must be so significant that it would have led to a different outcome before the RPD.

However, as the Court noted in Singh, the RAD context is considerably different. The RAD is not restricted to making a new assessment of the risk faced by the Appellant, though this could occur as a result of new evidence presented upon appeal. The RAD appeal is meant to be decided within four or five months of the RPD's decision. The Appellant may challenge the decision of the RPD, and the RAD has broad powers to review that decision for errors of fact or law, or mixed fact and law, to confirm the decision, to confirm on other grounds, to set aside the decision and substitute another, or to set aside the determination and refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination. It is of paramount importance that the RAD may look only to admissible new evidence when considering whether to hold a hearing under Section 110(6).37

The Court's definition of materiality, which is appropriate for evidence presented in support of a PRRA application, seems overly restrictive when applied to evidence submitted in an appeal to the RAD. If the RAD would apply the materiality factor as set out in Raza, it could lead to the rejection of evidence that is capable of showing that the RPD's decision was in error, only because that evidence is not so strong that it would have resulted in the acceptance of the refugee claim had the evidence been before the RPD. Further, the RAD is not asking-as the PRRA officer is under Raza-whether the RPD decision would have been different. The RAD is considering whether the RAD thinks the determination should have been different or whether the RPD decision was in error.

For example, it is not uncommon for the RPD to reject a refugee claim on the basis that the claimant has not established his or her identity, and in such situations, the RPD is not required to go further to consider the evidence of persecution.38 A claimant rejected by the RPD on the basis of identity-perhaps because identity documents were still in transit from the country of origin at the time of the refugee hearing-might appeal to the RAD and present as new evidence such recently-received documents. However, those documents might be rejected by the RAD if it considers their materiality as defined in Raza: whether the refugee claim would probably have succeeded if the documents were made available to the RPD. In many cases, the establishment of identity does not in and of itself warrant the acceptance of a refugee claim, and therefore the Appellant's newly-obtained identity documents could be rejected by the RAD as lacking materiality.

In the RAD's view, this restrictive approach to materiality is not consistent with the broad powers given to the RAD. While the PRRA officer is required to focus on a single issue-risk to the applicant-the RAD is required to consider both whether the RPD decision is in error and, after having reviewed all of the evidence, whether the Appellant is a protected person. An approach that focuses on whether the evidence is material enough to affect the outcome of the RAD appeal rather than the RPD's decision is therefore preferred.

For these reasons, the RAD will apply the following factors to evidence that passes the test in Section 110(4). a. The RAD will consider whether the proposed new evidence is credible and trustworthy. b. The RAD will assess the relevance of the evidence-whether it is capable, together with the other evidence in the record (including other admissible new evidence) of proving or disproving a fact at issue in either the refugee claim or the appeal.39 c. The RAD will determine whether the evidence is material, in the sense that it would be capable of justifying, with or without the benefit of an oral hearing, as the case may be, a disposition under section 111 of IRPA.

If the proposed new evidence does not meet each of the factors above, the RAD may choose not to admit it. These factors, however, are not exhaustive, as the RAD may consider other factors as appropriate in the circumstances.

The principal Appellant's proposed new evidence includes letters from human rights organizations in Uganda, from his wife, who is allegedly a parliamentarian in Uganda, as well as from organizations in Canada, which attest to his activities here and to his discussion of his bisexuality.40 These documents are dated after the rejection of the Appellants' refugee claims and therefore appear to meet the requirements of Section 110(4). However, the RAD declines to admit them, as they are not material in this appeal, in the sense that they are not capable of justifying a disposition under Section 111 of IRPA. While the documents speak to a number of issues relevant to his claim-including his activism and his sexual orientation-the RAD has already identified errors in the RPD's treatment of these issues. The documents cannot, however, do little to assist the RAD in considering the identity of the principal Appellant's sister and children, which in the RAD's view are significant issues here. The RAD notes that the Appellant's wife's affidavit does refer to the children; however, this in itself is not sufficient to address the RAD's concerns about their identity, nor does the principal Appellant's proposed new evidence resolve the issue of his delay in claiming, or his failure to include his arrests in his immigration forms.

The associated Appellant also asks the RAD to admit new evidence, including an expired passport, a 2010 letter from the Forum for Democratic Change (FDC), a 2011 letter from a presidential candidate, a 2014 letter from the FDC, a statutory declaration from a friend of her husband, a 2014 letter from the Division Police Headquarters in respect of her husband, and a statutory declaration from a member of the FDC.

These documents might be of assistance in the assessment of the associated Appellant's credibility, but do little to assist the determination of her personal identity. As such, even if these documents meet the test in Section 110(4), they are not material in that they could not justify a disposition under Section 111. Even if this proposed new evidence was admitted, it would not be capable of resolving the issue of the associated Appellant's identity, which must be considered again by the RPD.
For these reasons, the Appellants' proposed new evidence is not admissible in these appeals. Disposition

The RAD has found that the RPD erred in its assessment of the principal Appellant's credibility, and in its consideration of the remaining Appellants' identity. The RPD's decision must therefore be set aside. The RAD is unable to substitute its own determination, however, as concerns remain about the identity of all of the Appellants other than the principal Appellant. As the principal Appellant claims to be related to the other Appellants, and vouches for their identity, his own credibility is affected by the issue of their identity.

This matter must be heard by a differently-constituted panel of the RPD. As the identity of the children and the associated Appellant remains at issue, the RAD directs the RPD to appoint an independent designated representative for the minor Appellants.
Although the RAD has not accepted the Appellants' proposed new evidence in this appeal, they are not precluded from submitting such evidence to the RPD in accordance with that Division's Rules.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(c) of IRPA, the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel, subject to the directions set out above.
